title: Lecture 04 - Online/offline indicator, Redis vs DynamoDB, connection pooling, database and caching

questions.q: Can the systems discussed in the course be implemented without massive infrastructure, and what part of each system should you implement?
questions.answer: Yes: every single system discussed is implementable on a local machine. Implement the core of each system (e.g. the flash-sale module), not the whole thing with CRUD APIs and UI, because the devil lies in the details and implementing shows where the system can falter.

questions.q: Why does implementing the core of a system matter more than drawing boxes, according to the teacher?
questions.answer: Because when you implement it you realize where the system could falter and what challenges come with implementation; in real organizations you are expected to implement, not just draw boxes.

questions.q: What two items were on the agenda for the second half of this session, and what example application were they discussed in?
questions.answer: Databases and caching, discussed in the context of designing a multi-user blogging platform like Medium.

questions.q: Why did the teacher say the online/offline indicator would be designed without worrying much about scale?
questions.answer: Because it is day one; the design changes a lot once other concepts (sharding etc.) are covered in later weeks, so the focus is first principles and intuition, with some performance improvements but not scale.

questions.q: What is the 'spiral' approach to building a system, and what is usually its core?
questions.answer: Decide the core of the system (the single point of focus that makes it possible) and build everything around it as needed. The core is use-case specific: most often the database (schema), but it can be the communication layer, e.g. WebSockets for a messaging app.

questions.q: List the steps of the 'incremental building' approach in the order written on the board, and say which step the loop arrow returns to.
questions.answer: 1. Start with a day-zero architecture; 2. see how each component would behave under load and at scale; 3. identify the bottleneck; 4. re-architect; 5. repeat. The loop arrow runs from 'repeat' back to step 2.

questions.q: When do you typically choose the spiral approach versus incremental building?
questions.answer: Spiral when the system is simple/no-brainer and you have built similar systems before, so you know how things will transpire. Incremental when you are in an ambiguous, uncertain situation, e.g. a startup: push a day-zero architecture to users and re-architect over time.

questions.q: What simple day-zero architecture did the teacher give as an example for incremental building?
questions.answer: User, load balancer, API server, database; then check whether a server is overburdened and whether to split it into another service.

questions.q: What are the three 'points to remember' written on the board before the online/offline design began?
questions.answer: Understand the core property and access pattern; affinity towards a tech comes second; build an intuition towards building systems.

questions.q: What misconception about choosing technology did the teacher warn against at the start of the design?
questions.answer: Having a rigid affinity for a particular tech ('I'll only use Redis/Postgres/DynamoDB/Cassandra'). Instead pick on the core property/access pattern you need; e.g. if your company is not on AWS you cannot use DynamoDB, and many systems people build on Cassandra can be built on a relational DB.

questions.q: In the first storage model for the indicator, what types were stored and what access pattern did it reveal?
questions.answer: user → online/offline: the user ID as an int and the status as a bool (true = online). The access pattern is key-value (get status for one user, for a set of users, update one user's status); the DB was still not decided.

questions.q: What is the first critical API design decision for rendering statuses, and why?
questions.answer: Expose a batch endpoint (GET /status/users?ids=u1,u2,u3,u4) that takes many user IDs and returns all their statuses, instead of only a per-user endpoint; otherwise rendering four users needs four API calls from the front end. Batching reduces network calls and keeps heavy lifting on the backend.

questions.q: In the 'Interfacing API' diagram, what are the components and how are they connected?
questions.answer: User (with a device) ⟷ API Server ⟷ Database, both arrows double-headed.

questions.q: Why can't the API server use a pull-based model to learn whether a user is online?
questions.answer: HTTP is stateless and there is no persistent connection, so the API server cannot proactively talk to the client; the client has to push its status (unless there is a persistent connection).

questions.q: What endpoint do clients use to report they are alive, and what does it do?
questions.answer: POST /heartbeat: the authenticated user is marked as alive. Every user periodically sends a heartbeat to the service.

questions.q: Why isn't it enough to send one call when the user comes online and one when they log out?
questions.answer: Because you cannot reliably tell when you go offline: the device may crash, run out of battery or be unplugged with no chance to make a final API call, so the UI would keep showing the user online. Hence periodic heartbeats are needed.

questions.q: When is a user considered offline in the heartbeat design, and how long is 'long enough'?
questions.answer: When no heartbeat has been received for long enough. 'Long enough' is subjective/business logic, configured per system (10 s, 1 min, 10 min...); the class used 30 seconds.

questions.q: How did the stored data change once heartbeats were introduced?
questions.answer: Instead of a bool, store the time the last heartbeat was received: table pulse(user_id, last_hb), last_hb in epoch seconds. Every heartbeat runs UPDATE pulse SET last_hb = NOW() WHERE user_id = u1.

questions.q: The teacher draws tables and writes SQL on the board. Does that mean the design uses a relational database?
questions.answer: No. A table drawing only helps visualize the schema and SQL is just an easy way to express it; you can model it however you want.

questions.q: State the getStatus business logic rules in order.
questions.answer: If there is no entry in the DB for the user → offline (user never came online). If there is an entry and entry.last_hb < now() - 30 s → offline. Otherwise → online. Same holds for the batch endpoint.

questions.q: How often did the board say a user sends a heartbeat?
questions.answer: Every 10 seconds.

questions.q: How large is each row of the pulse table and why?
questions.answer: 8 bytes: two columns, user_id and last_hb (epoch seconds), each a 4-byte int.

questions.q: What is the total storage for 1 billion users and what does it tell you about the system?
questions.answer: 1B entries × 8 B = 8 GB. Storage is not the challenge (it fits in the RAM of a cheap machine; a phone has 128 GB); the system needs something else.

questions.q: Even though storage is not a problem, why did the teacher still ask 'can we do better on storage?'
questions.answer: At every step you should ask critical questions and consider alternatives, because design is about analyzing trade-offs; documenting every possibility (and why you chose one path) is what makes a better senior engineer.

questions.q: What is the 'absence == offline' idea and how does it reduce storage?
questions.answer: The user only sees green/grey, so if the entry exists the user is online and if it doesn't they are offline. Expire/delete entries 30 s after the last heartbeat, so the table only holds active users: total entries = active users.

questions.q: With absence == offline, what is the storage for 1B total users of whom 100k are active?
questions.answer: 100k entries, total size 800 KB.

questions.q: What was 'Approach 1' for deleting expired entries, and what were its drawbacks?
questions.answer: A cron job that scans for entries whose last_hb is older than 30 s and deletes them. Works for a startup but not robust: you must handle edge cases in business logic, and it adds another moving part/process whose uptime, monitoring and telemetry you must manage.

questions.q: What design warning did the teacher give about adding extra components like the cron job?
questions.answer: Never just draw boxes for the sake of it; think about implementing, monitoring and managing each component. Making your diagram look complex is the worst thing you can do; look for a simpler alternative.

questions.q: What was 'Approach 2' and which databases did the teacher name for it?
questions.answer: Offload expiration to the datastore ('never re-invent the wheel'): a DB with key-value access plus expiration (TTL), e.g. Redis or DynamoDB.

questions.q: With a TTL-based store, what happens on each heartbeat and what determines online/offline?
questions.answer: Each heartbeat updates the entry with TTL = 30 s, moving the expiration time forward. If no heartbeat arrives within 30 s, the DB deletes the key automatically. Entry exists → online; no entry → offline.

questions.q: In the Redis vs DynamoDB table, which column got the ticks for 'persistence' and 'managed', and what qualifier was added to 'managed'?
questions.answer: DynamoDB got both. 'Managed' was qualified with team size and expertise: a lean team offloads infrastructure management to the cloud vendor.

questions.q: What is vendor lock-in?
questions.answer: Being locked into a particular cloud vendor because the tool you use only exists there (e.g. DynamoDB only on AWS); moving clouds means rewriting a lot of code for another technology.

questions.q: Besides cost and security incidents, what 'very interesting' reason for avoiding vendor lock-in did the teacher add?
questions.answer: Competition: if your cloud vendor enters your business, your cloud bill funds your competitor (e.g. Swiggy/Zomato on AWS when Amazon launched food delivery). That's why Walmart is on GCP, not AWS.

questions.q: What counter-example did the teacher give to the competitor rule, and why?
questions.answer: Netflix stays on AWS despite Amazon Prime Video being a competitor, because moving out would mean rewriting too much code; it is AWS's biggest customer and likely gets a good deal.

questions.q: When does vendor lock-in not matter much for a company?
questions.answer: At an early startup with a small bill (e.g. $10k/month), it doesn't matter; it matters for big customers (e.g. $10M/month bills).

questions.q: Why do many companies prefer open-source technologies over proprietary ones?
questions.answer: To avoid being locked into a particular vendor.

questions.q: A student said DynamoDB gives persistence. What did the teacher say about Redis persistence?
questions.answer: Redis also gives persistence (AOF files, RDB files, configurable flush frequency), with some limitations; you should know how it is done, not just that it exists.

questions.q: Which column of the table did 'vendor lock-in' and 'future extensibility' go to, and what Redis features make it extensible?
questions.answer: Redis. It has many data structures beyond key-value (Bloom filters, HyperLogLog, geospatial queries), useful if future features need them.

questions.q: Is it true that Redis only stores strings while DynamoDB has numbers?
questions.answer: No: Redis has numbers too and a bunch of data structures.

questions.q: What did the teacher say about databases' features converging?
questions.answer: Every database is adding features: DynamoDB has streams, Redis gives CDC, MongoDB supports ACID, SQL databases support sharding. Go in depth into each candidate's pros and cons before deciding.

questions.q: Why is Redis better for time sensitivity than DynamoDB, according to the teacher (it is not only because it is in-memory)?
questions.answer: Redis supports persistent connections, giving extreme low latency; DynamoDB is stateless (no persistent connections). Redis also gives hooks telling you immediately that a key expired, whereas DynamoDB only gives that through streams, which take longer to process.

questions.q: Name the final five rows of the Redis vs DynamoDB table and which side each favoured.
questions.answer: DynamoDB: persistence; managed (team size & expertise). Redis: vendor lock-in; future extensibility; time sensitivity.

questions.q: Why do teams go for managed services?
questions.answer: Lean teams (5-10 people) don't want the pressure of managing infrastructure, or lack expertise; managing any database comes with pain points (observability, profiling). Managed services make it easy.

questions.q: How are online/offline indicators actually built in the real world?
questions.answer: With WebSockets (plus a lot of tuning and optimization), not the day-one HTTP heartbeat design.

questions.q: How many requests per minute does the heartbeat design generate for 1 million active users, and what does each cause?
questions.answer: Heartbeat every 10 s → 6 per user per minute → 6 million requests per minute; each heartbeat results in one DB call, so the DB must handle 6 million updates per minute.

questions.q: For this system, which is the challenge: storage or computation?
questions.answer: Computation (the number of queries/updates), not storage: the whole data fits in 8 GB.

questions.q: How many network trips does setting up and tearing down a TCP connection cost, and why does this matter here?
questions.answer: Five: three-way handshake to set up, two-way teardown. With each request opening a new DB connection, this is expensive; the board called 'creating a new connection every time' the hectic part.

questions.q: What is a connection pool?
questions.answer: The API server pre-establishes a set of TCP connections to the DB (e.g. 3 at startup) and keeps them open; each query picks a free connection, marks it unavailable, fires the query and returns it, avoiding setup/teardown per request.

questions.q: The number of queries stays the same with a connection pool. Why does it still reduce load on the database?
questions.answer: Establishing/terminating TCP connections costs the DB CPU and network bandwidth (reading handshake packets, OS buffers); reusing pre-established connections saves that work, which dominates for micro updates.

questions.q: List the benefits of connection pooling the teacher gave.
questions.answer: Faster API response (saves 5 network trips: just one request and one response), lower DB load freeing it for other queries, lower infrastructure cost.

questions.q: What happens when all pooled connections are busy and a new request arrives?
questions.answer: Either it waits for a connection to be freed, or it creates a new TCP connection, fires the query and adds the connection to the pool (stretching the pool on demand) up to a configured maximum; beyond the max it must wait.

questions.q: Why do connection pools need a maximum size and an idle TTL?
questions.answer: Every DB has a limit on TCP connections; hundreds of servers each holding 100 connections can exhaust it. The max caps per-server connections (e.g. min 3, max 100) and an idle TTL (e.g. 10 min unused) terminates unused connections.

questions.q: Is a connection pool a separate service? How is it implemented?
questions.answer: No. It is a library running inside the API server: on boot it creates multiple DB connection objects and puts them in a blocking queue; callers pop a connection, or wait (loop) until one is put back.

questions.q: When does a connection pool give a massive boost, and when is the benefit outweighed?
questions.answer: Massive boost for micro queries such as a one-row update by primary key. For big SQL queries whose run time is long, execution time outweighs connection setup so the benefit is small. In general having a pool is always a good option.

questions.q: What other system can be built with the same pattern as the online/offline indicator?
questions.answer: Failure detection in a distributed system: nodes send heartbeats to a central server that tracks which are alive (e.g. detecting EC2 machines down, or a load balancer detecting dead backends).

questions.q: If a new API server cannot get a DB connection because the DB hit its TCP connection limit, what happens?
questions.answer: It waits, retrying until an existing server terminates a connection. The fix is to scale the DB to handle more connections (vertically, or by sharding).

questions.q: What is the most common bottleneck of a database, according to the teacher, and how does concurrency relate to DB size?
questions.answer: The maximum number of connections it can handle. The concurrency you want to support determines the concurrent connections the DB must handle, which determines DB size; beyond that scale vertically, or shard.

questions.q: Self-hosted Redis vs DynamoDB for a small team that needs to autoscale: what order of choice did the teacher give?
questions.answer: With a lean team without expertise go for DynamoDB or another managed solution; next option is managed Redis (Redis Labs, AWS, GCP); self-host only if you have team expertise and engineering bandwidth. Otherwise throw money at the cloud provider.

questions.q: If a pool has max 100 and some connections expired, what happens when demand rises again? Are there always 100 connections?
questions.answer: New connections are created on demand and added to the pool with the same expiration; there are at most 100, and the actual number depends on incoming requests.

questions.q: Why is the number of connections the key factor in scaling the DB for this system?
questions.answer: Reads and writes are micro (one row by key, no big analytics query), so the bottleneck becomes the network, specifically establishing TCP connections. Board: micro reads/updates → hence network bottleneck.

questions.q: When would you not stress on connections and focus elsewhere?
questions.answer: When queries are heavy (aggregations, 10-15 table joins) and take longer than establishing a connection; then focus on the CPU and memory side of the DB.

questions.q: How do you find how many concurrent connections a database can handle?
questions.answer: It depends on RAM and the network card. Managed services (e.g. AWS RDS) give a formula/show it in the UI/docs; self-managed: benchmark (it also depends on load). Often you need instances with dedicated/high network bandwidth.

questions.q: What are the four things in computer science that determine scaling, with an example of each?
questions.answer: Memory, CPU, disk and network (GPU counts as CPU). CPU: massive aggregations; memory: big joins pulling lots of data; disk: storing large data, e.g. data warehouses; network: number of queries a machine can serve.

questions.q: How do you set the minimum and maximum size of a connection pool?
questions.answer: Minimum: typically 3 or 5. Maximum: DB max connections ÷ max number of servers at any time (e.g. 1000 / 100 = 10), padded since some servers get more traffic (e.g. 15); a practice is about 1.2x the average. Start conservative, monitor pool metrics (about a week of production), retune.

questions.q: After setting initial pool sizes, how should you tune them, and what should you monitor?
questions.answer: Start with a conservative setting, observe metrics, then retune. Monitor how the pool performs: the number of connections in the pool at any moment and the number of servers; about one week of production data gives the numbers to tune on.

questions.q: For a festival with 2x users, how should you handle the connection load?
questions.answer: Vertically scale the DB so it supports the needed concurrent requests (and scale back down later), then tune the connection pool maximum; have the right monitoring.

questions.q: What are the six foundational components to think about when designing systems?
questions.answer: Database, caching, scaling, delegation, concurrency, communication. Any decision affects one of these 6 factors.

questions.q: Describe the schema of the blogging platform.
questions.answer: users: id, name, bio. blogs: id, author_id, title, body, published_at, is_deleted. One user can write multiple blogs; multiple users.

questions.q: What happens when a user deletes a blog with soft delete?
questions.answer: Instead of DELETE you UPDATE: set is_deleted = true.

questions.q: What are the three key reasons for soft delete, in the order on the board?
questions.answer: Recoverability, archival, audit.

questions.q: What example illustrates recoverability?
questions.answer: Google Drive: a deleted file goes to trash for 30 days and can be recovered during that time.

questions.q: How does soft delete enable archival?
questions.answer: Deleted user content is valuable (e.g. for ML training); soft delete, then a job collects soft-deleted rows into S3 / blob storage.

questions.q: What real story illustrated the audit reason?
questions.answer: A user harassed another online and deleted the comment after a police complaint; the police asked the platform for details. With soft delete the evidence was still there; the teacher visited the police station with printed traces.

questions.q: Why is soft delete 'easy on the database engine'?
questions.answer: Most storage engines use B+ trees; a hard delete removes the entry and can unbalance the tree, forcing rebalancing that costs CPU. Soft delete only updates a column, so no rebalancing.

questions.q: How does the DB store a LONGTEXT column vs a VARCHAR column?
questions.answer: VARCHAR (short text) is stored inline with the other columns in the (fixed-width) row. LONGTEXT is stored at a separate disk location with only a reference in the row, so reading it costs an extra disk read.

questions.q: Which fields of the blogging schema are short text and which long text, and why not make everything inline?
questions.answer: Bio, email, names are VARCHAR; blog body (and long comments, e.g. 5000 chars = 5000 bytes) are long text. Keep rows small so they scan easily; the body is only needed when someone opens the blog page, while listings need title/excerpt.

questions.q: What are the three ways to store date-time on the board, in order?
questions.answer: Datetime as datetime; datetime as epoch integer; datetime as custom format (int), YYYYMMDD.

questions.q: Why can a native datetime type be slow for a query like published_at > now() - 7 days?
questions.answer: If the DB serializes it as a string on disk, it must read each value, parse it into a datetime object (year, month, day, hour, minute, second) and compare. Each DB stores it differently (MySQL, Postgres, MongoDB...; some as epoch seconds/ms), so check yours.

questions.q: What labels did the board attach to 'datetime as datetime'?
questions.answer: Convenient; sub-optimal; heavy on size and index; serialized in some format.

questions.q: What is an epoch integer, and how much space does it save compared with the string?
questions.answer: Seconds (or ms) elapsed since 1 January 1970. The string '02-04-2022T09:01:36Z' takes about 20 bytes; the integer takes 4 bytes.

questions.q: What is the trade-off of storing date-time as an epoch integer?
questions.answer: Efficient, optimal, lightweight on index (plain integer comparison), but not readable: you cannot tell the time by looking at it.

questions.q: What did Redbus do in 2016 with date-time and why?
questions.answer: A datetime column caused a performance bottleneck through massive date comparisons. They needed readability (they viewed raw values in IDEs/UI) and only date-level granularity, so they stored the date as an integer in YYYYMMDD format (e.g. 20220402): readable and fast integer comparison/index.

questions.q: Does the YYYYMMDD integer perform better than an epoch integer?
questions.answer: No: both are integers with the same performance; the custom format only adds readability. It was a company/use-case choice (analytics, not transactional).

questions.q: What does storing epoch time lose compared with a datetime, and how do you handle it?
questions.answer: Time zone information. Store in Unix/UTC and render in the device's local time zone; be careful to take everything in UTC.

questions.q: If soft-deleted rows are eventually hard-deleted, is the no-rebalancing benefit lost?
questions.answer: No. Batch the hard deletes: e.g. deleting 100 rows at once and committing triggers one rebalance instead of up to 100, cutting rebalances by the batch size.

questions.q: What limitation of a 4-byte epoch integer was raised, and what did the teacher recommend reading?
questions.answer: A 4-byte integer maxes out soon (teacher said around 2032); 8 bytes doubles space, and pre-1970 dates need negative values. Read MySQL's official datetime docs: it stores datetime compactly (~6 bytes) over a huge range (BCE to ~20,000 years).

questions.q: What is caching, according to the teacher's definition?
questions.answer: Anything that saves a heavy computation or expensive operation: disk I/O, network I/O or computation. Memoization in dynamic programming is caching.

questions.q: Are caches only RAM based? Give an example otherwise.
questions.answer: No: disk or even network can be a cache. E.g. caching on local disk to avoid an expensive network call.

questions.q: What are caches fundamentally, according to the board?
questions.answer: Glorified hash tables (key-value), some with advanced data structures (Redis: HyperLogLog, Bloom filters, geo).

questions.q: Describe the blogging platform diagram with the cache.
questions.answer: Users → LB → three API servers → Database; one central cache that all three API servers connect to (the cache sits logically between API and DB).

questions.q: Describe the read path through the central cache.
questions.answer: API server checks the cache; on hit return; on miss read from DB, put it in the cache, return to the user.

questions.q: Why use a central remote cache for the blogging platform?
questions.answer: Every request, whichever API server it hits, reads the same single copy; it saves expensive DB queries (e.g. 3-4 table joins for a popular blog) and cuts DB load massively.

questions.q: What was the 'fun exercise' for the next class?
questions.answer: Find possible places that can be used as a cache with an example (e.g. central RAM cache for app-level data saves DB computations; think CDN, load balancer).

questions.q: Can the DB itself hold pre-computed results as a cache?
questions.answer: Yes, that is a possible place: ask 'why not this?'; caching isn't limited to RAM.

questions.q: Soft-deleted rows grow the DB. What do you do?
questions.answer: Periodic hard delete (e.g. once a day) of soft-deleted rows, or move them elsewhere (archival).

questions.q: What does GDPR's right to be forgotten require, and how soon?
questions.answer: A user can ask the company to delete everything about them; the company must hard delete within roughly a month (a time buffer).

questions.q: In practice, is data fully removed after a right-to-be-forgotten request?
questions.answer: No: PII is hard-deleted from the transactional systems and tracked places, but logs and historical DB snapshots keep data (nobody updates all snapshots). Atlassian recovered hard-deleted data in 14 days during an outage.

questions.q: Should a cache compress data, and where?
questions.answer: Trade-off: decompression cost vs memory. Worth it for large blobs (e.g. 10 KB to 1 KB), not small fields like email. Do it in the application before sending, so you also save network bandwidth; the cache shouldn't offer compression.

questions.q: An interviewer said a background job hard-deleting soft-deleted rows would cause downtime because of locking. How did the teacher answer?
questions.answer: Deleting causes no downtime of the service; do staggered deletions at a linear pace. Locking rows while deleting is about strong consistency (avoiding stale reads of a deleted entry), not availability.

questions.q: If the same pre-computed result is stored in Redis and in a database table, what decides which is faster to read?
questions.answer: Both use persistent connections, so that cancels out. Redis reads from memory in one hashed lookup; a disk-based DB traverses a B+ tree on disk (about log n reads). For tiny reads disk is much slower, for larger reads (e.g. 1 KB) the gap is small. RAM is more expensive and limits cache size (disk allows a larger cache), and using the main DB adds load to existing requests. Overall not much difference; it is a trade-off.

questions.q: How should you hard delete 100,000 soft-deleted rows without hurting a busy database?
questions.answer: Do staggered deletion, like garbage collection: never delete them all in one shot; spread it across the day, e.g. an hourly job deleting about 10,000 rows per run.

questions.q: A table has a unique index on email and uses soft delete. A user deletes their account and wants to sign up again with the same email. What must you do?
questions.answer: In this use case the row has to be hard deleted (a soft-deleted row would block the new account).

questions.q: Instead of a cron job, can you set a retention policy in the DB to delete old rows? Which approach is better for DB performance?
questions.answer: Yes; then the DB runs a thread doing the cron job for you (you offload it to the database). Best: offload it to the database and delete in a staggered way.

questions.q: If the cached field in the DB is indexed, isn't it read from RAM, making the DB as fast as Redis?
questions.answer: Only in the best case, when the table/index is small enough for the DB to keep in RAM; then there is no difference. Always reason about the worst case: if RAM can't hold the index, it is a disk read.

questions.q: If you work at Google and will always use GCP, does vendor lock-in matter? What other concern might a manager still have?
questions.answer: No: you are your own vendor (or always on one cloud), so lock-in is out of the picture. But a manager weighs how easy it is to hire talent: many developers know an open-source tech like Neo4j, few know a proprietary one like TigerGraph.

questions.q: Why wasn't availability one of the rows comparing Redis and DynamoDB?
questions.answer: It was assumed equal: availability is a property of the engineers (expertise to run it), not of the database. With DynamoDB AWS provides it; with self-hosted Redis your engineers must.

questions.q: How would you support showing 'last seen' in the online/offline design?
questions.answer: It was out of scope. If you need it, you cannot delete the rows: keep them, and the last heartbeat received is the last-seen time. Whether to show it is a product call; storage (8 GB) is not a problem anyway.

questions.q: Are soft delete and archival the same thing?
questions.answer: No. Soft delete allows you to archive: you have time to collect soft-deleted rows later (e.g. after a day), move them elsewhere, then hard delete. Hard deleting and immediately copying to S3 would be slow.

questions.q: Is it fine to use Redis as the primary database for the online/offline indicator?
questions.answer: Yes. Configure AOF-based persistence for on-disk persistence, and the data is small enough (8 GB) to fit in RAM. The choice depends on the guarantees the system needs, not stereotypes about what a DB is for.

questions.q: Should autoscaling for sudden surges count against self-managed Redis versus DynamoDB?
questions.answer: Yes, as one more point: self-hosting needs engineering expertise to manage, scale and react to surges, an added strain on the team. With a lean team, offload to DynamoDB: you pay them and they become your extended engineering team.

questions.q: Should you avoid database-specific features like TTL so you can switch databases later?
questions.answer: No: you picked the DB because you needed expiration. Other DBs offer similar features, or you can re-implement them (a cron job; Debezium CDC instead of DynamoDB streams). Document the migration steps and know your design's limitations, but draw a line and stop overthinking, or you end up writing your own database.

questions.q: What did the teacher recommend for understanding how connection pooling behaves when the database is scaled?
questions.answer: Write a hello-world with a connection pool against a local database to see its configuration options and limitations; horizontal scaling of databases is covered the next week.

questions.q: What is the downside of a connection pool configured with a minimum of 100 connections per server when the DB supports at most 1000?
questions.answer: It limits how many API servers you can run: about 10 servers use up the DB's 1000 connections, so adding 20 more during a spike fails. The pool configuration and the DB's max connections cap the number of servers.

questions.q: What goes wrong if pools may grow freely and the idle-connection TTL is very long (e.g. 10 minutes)?
questions.answer: Existing servers keep hogging DB connections; new servers added for load cannot get connections, and users routed to them see an outage.

questions.q: What conservative starting configuration for a connection pool did the teacher recommend?
questions.answer: Start with a minimum of 3 or 5 connections and let it grow to a limit, maybe under 50 or 100. The idle TTL must be neither too short nor too long (too long leaves many unused connections); find the sweet spot for your use case.

questions.q: What single metric matters most for tuning a connection pool, and why?
questions.answer: Average SQL query completion time on the database: long-running queries keep connections open longer, so the TTL can't be short and the pool may need to grow.

questions.q: Using TTL saves space but makes Redis do deletions. Is that computation a concern?
questions.answer: No: in-memory deletion is peanuts for Redis. TTL was used because space mattered; if space doesn't matter, skip it and keep the entries.

questions.q: HTTP is stateless. Does that mean HTTP connections can never stay open?
questions.answer: No. HTTP is stateless (one request, one response), but connections can persist: the keep-alive header tells the web server not to terminate it, HTTP/2 keeps persistent connections, and WebSocket (not HTTP) does too. For design, think of HTTP as stateless and use better options (WebSockets, MQTT) when you need state.

questions.q: What is the relationship between HTTP and TCP?
questions.answer: HTTP is a protocol/specification that usually runs on top of TCP (a layer-4 protocol); they are independent, and you could send HTTP messages over UDP too.
